result:
I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the strange intimacy of watching strangers live their lives through windows, and what it reveals about our hunger for connection.

---

The Window Exchange

I moved to a new apartment six months ago, on the fourth floor of a building that faces another building across a narrow courtyard. The gap between us is maybe thirty feet. Close enough to see clearly, far enough to maintain the polite fiction of privacy. I didn't think much about it until winter came, when darkness arrived before I finished work and everyone turned on their lights.

Now I know the rhythms of six different apartments without knowing a single name.

There's the woman on the second floor who dances while she cooks. She wears headphones and moves with complete abandon, stirring something on the stove while her hips sway to music I can't hear. Sometimes she sings, mouth open wide, performing for no one. I catch myself smiling. She's the reason I don't close my blinds at six o'clock anymore.

Above her, an elderly man sits in a recliner every evening, reading under a lamp with a green glass shade. The lamp makes his white hair glow strangely, like he's underwater. He turns pages slowly, methodically. I've never seen him look up from his book. I wonder what he's reading, if it's the same novel stretched across weeks or if he devours paperbacks whole. I imagine him as a retired professor, or perhaps a former sailor, though I have no evidence for either.

The third-floor couple fights in their kitchen. Not often, but with a particular intensity that makes me step back from my own window, embarrassed to witness. She gestures with her hands. He leans against the counter with his arms crossed. Once I saw him cry, shoulders shaking, while she held him. The next night they were making dinner together, laughing. I don't know what to make of them. Maybe that's the point—I'm making nothing of them, just watching fragments without context, trying to assemble whole humans from scattered scenes.

Across and to the left, a family with two small children has Christmas lights still strung in their window in March. The kids press their faces to the glass sometimes, looking out at the courtyard, at my building, at nothing in particular. One of them waved at me last week. I waved back. Then we both disappeared, me ducking behind my curtain, them probably called away by a parent. The moment felt illicit, though we did nothing wrong.

I tell myself I'm not really watching. I'm just existing near a window, and they happen to be visible. This is the lie of urban life, the unspoken contract: we agree to be seen in exchange for seeing, to surrender true privacy for the comfort of proximity. The city is made of such negotiations.

But here's what I've realized: I'm not watching them so much as I'm watching *someone*. The specificity hardly matters. What I crave is the evidence of other lives continuing, parallel to mine, equally real and complex and mundane. When I see the dancing woman burn something and curse, when I see the old man mark his place and remove his glasses to rub his eyes, I feel less alone in my own small routines. The loneliness of modern life isn't always the absence of people. Sometimes it's the presence of too many people you can't reach, separated by glass and air and the invisible walls we build to protect ourselves.

My grandmother used to talk about life in her village, where everyone knew everyone, where privacy was impossible and no one expected it. She described it as suffocating, the constant observation, the impossibility of reinventing yourself or hiding your failures. She moved to the city as soon as she could. I wonder what she would make of my window-gazing, this voluntary return to village intimacy without village accountability. I don't have to bring soup when the old man is sick. I don't have to explain myself to the dancing woman if I miss her performance for a week. I'm a ghost in their lives, and they're ghosts in mine—present but not participating, visible but not tangible.

There's a word in Japanese, *komorebi*, for sunlight filtering through trees. I've heard another, *kawatare-doki*, for the twilight hour when it's neither day nor night, when shapes blur and the world becomes uncertain. I want a word for the feeling of watching strangers through windows, this particular blend of connection and isolation, of care and intrusion. Maybe we don't have one because we're not supposed to admit we do it. We're supposed to close our blinds and mind our business and consume our entertainments in manufactured, packaged forms—television shows about fictional people, social media profiles carefully curated, podcasts where strangers discuss their lives with professional intimacy.

The window offers something rawer, unedited. The man on the third floor doesn't know he's performing his grief. The children don't know they're part of my evening. There's no narrative arc, no resolution, no promise of meaning. Just life, accumulating in ordinary moments, visible to anyone who happens to look up at the right time.

I think about the physics of it. Light leaves their windows, travels across the courtyard, enters my eyes. Photons that bounced off their skin, their books, their burning dinners, now become part of me, literally, absorbed or processed into neural signals. In a physical sense, I carry pieces of them. They carry pieces of me too, if they ever look this way. We're exchanging matter constantly, becoming each other in microscopic ways, maintaining the illusion of separation through architecture and habit.

Last week, the dancing woman saw me watching. I was obvious about it, standing right at the glass with a cup of tea. She paused, headphones still on, mid-stir. We looked at each other across the gap. I raised my cup in what I hoped was a friendly, non-creepy gesture. She laughed— I saw her shoulders shake, her head tilt back—then she curtsied, actually curtsied, and resumed her dancing with even more dramatic flair, spinning, pointing at me, inviting the audience in.

Now I dance too, sometimes, when I'm certain she's there. We perform for each other across the void, two strangers who have never spoken, connected by light and movement and the shared understanding that loneliness is easier when you can see someone else being lonely too, when you can pretend for a moment that your windows are doors, that the gap is bridgeable, that the distance is just space and not the fundamental condition of being alive among others who are equally, terribly, beautifully alone.

I still don't know her name. I hope I never learn it. Some intimacies depend on remaining incomplete.
